 Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America | Antibiotics Deconstructed | Bench to Bedside With SIDP | Antimicrobial Stewardship | Hepatitis Advertisement News | Articles | October 19, 2026 Raw Cheddar Cheese Recall Flags Non-O157 E coli 
 The company, Family Farmstead Dairy, issued a raw cheddar recall over potential contamination with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) is happening across 7 states.
 Advertisement Family Farmstead Dairy, LLC, of Worcester, New York, is recalling a single lot of its Raw Mild Cheddar Cheese over potential contamination with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC).¹ Testing identified two non-O157 serotypes, E coli O26:H11 and O45:H2. No illnesses have been reported to date.¹
 The company issued a corrected release revising both the serotype and the distribution pattern, after the initial version cited E coli O157:H7.¹ Federal rules permit interstate sale of raw milk cheese only after aging for at least 60 days at temperatures no lower than 35 °F.² Raw cheddar drew similar scrutiny in early 2024, when the CDC investigated a multistate E coli outbreak linked to Raw Farm brand raw cheddar and the company issued a voluntary recall.³
 The recalled product carries lot code and best-by date 7/22/27.¹ Family Farmstead distributed the cheese to grocers in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and Massachusetts.¹ The announcement cautions downstream distributors may have shipped the product to additional states, and no other Family Farmstead products are affected.¹
 The contamination surfaced through a Maryland sample collected under the FDA Laboratory Flexible Funding Model (LFFM) program.¹ Analysis isolated two STEC strains from two samples of Family Farmstead A2 Raw Cheddar in 8-oz packages bearing the same 7/22/27 code.¹ Because detection came through product surveillance sampling rather than an illness cluster, the recall began ahead of any reported cases.¹
 Consumers should not eat the product and should discard it or return it to the place of purchase for a full refund.¹ The company has received no reports of illness associated with the recalled lot.¹ Family Farmstead stated it is working to identify the cause of the contamination and to implement corrective actions.¹
 astro-island:empty]:hidden [&:has(>astro-island:empty)+*]:-mt-8"> What You Need to Know
 Family Farmstead Dairy recalled one lot of Raw Mild Cheddar Cheese (lot code and best-by date 7/22/27) after Maryland surveillance testing isolated STEC O26:H11 and O45:H2.
 The cheese reached grocers in seven eastern states and may have spread further through downstream distributors, though no illnesses have been reported.
 Antibiotics are generally not recommended for suspected STEC infection because of a possible link to HUS, so management centers on supportive care and HUS monitoring.
 Clinical Presentation, HUS Risk, and Laboratory Diagnosis of Non-O157 STEC Infection
 O26 and O45 rank among the six non-O157 serogroups most commonly associated with STEC illness in the United States, along with O103, O111, O121, and O145.⁴ Non-O157 strains can cause illness resembling O157 infection.⁴ According to the company announcement, infection with the detected serotypes typically produces diarrheal illness, often with bloody stools.¹
 Most healthy adults recover within a week, but some patients develop hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a form of kidney failure most likely in young children and older adults.¹ HUS can lead to serious kidney damage and death.¹ Clinicians should monitor patients with confirmed STEC infection for signs of HUS.⁴
 Antibiotics are generally not recommended for STEC infection, since some studies associate antimicrobial use with HUS development and a treatment benefit has not been clearly demonstrated.⁴ Management therefore centers on supportive care and close observation for renal and hematologic complications.⁴
 Diagnosis of non-O157 STEC requires more than routine stool culture. Stool specimens from all patients with symptoms consistent with acute bacterial enteritis should be tested for Shiga toxin, with STEC culture attempted.⁴ Testing may use culture or a culture-independent diagnostic test detecting Shiga toxin 1 and/or 2 or its genes.⁴
 The Family Farmstead recall represents the latest STEC detection in raw milk cheese following the 2024 Raw Farm outbreak.³ No CDC outbreak investigation has been announced in connection with the recalled lot, and the company continues to report no associated illnesses.¹
